pr.title: unstably allow constants to refer to statics and read from immutable statics
pr.description:
I am not aware of any fundamental reason why we cannot allow constants to mention statics. What we really need is that constants do not *read from* statics that can change their value:
- This would break the principle that "constants behave as-if their expression was inlined everywhere and executed at runtime". This is enforced by halting const-eval interpretation when a read from a mutable global occurs.
- When building a valtree we want to be sure that the constant and everything it refers to is truly immutable. This is enforced by aborting valtree construction when a read from a mutable global occurs.

r? @oli-obk -- if you are okay with experimenting with this feature, I will create a tracking issue.
Based on and blocked on https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/119044; only the last commit is new.
pr.author: RalfJung

analysis.summary: Const evaluation (including the evaluation path used by ConstPropLint) must distinguish immutable-static access from mutable-global access when constants are allowed to mention statics. The historical blanket "constant accesses static" rejection is too strong for immutable statics, but simply removing it would let a const read mutable global memory or carry a final value pointing into mutable memory, breaking the as-if-inlined invariant and const-pattern/valtree soundness. The correct rule is mutability-based: allow reads of immutable statics, reject reads from mutable global memory, and have const validation recursively descend into referenced statics and reject a const value that references mutable or unvalidatable extern statics.
analysis.originalLogic: Before this PR, the const-eval machine had `can_access_statics: CanAccessStatics`; for consts it was `CanAccessStatics::No`. On global read access, if this flag was `No` and `static_def_id.is_some()`, evaluation returned `ConstEvalErrKind::ConstAccessesStatic` ("constant accesses static"), regardless of whether the static was mutable. Validation likewise rejected any pointer to a static from a const via `PtrToStatic`, and it did not recursively validate referenced statics: "We skip recursively checking other statics." The deleted const-prop regression test encoded this as `const TEST: u8 = MY_STATIC; //~ ERROR constant` with stderr `constant accesses static`.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect transformation is to treat "mentions/references a static" as the forbidden condition and thus remove the `static_def_id.is_some()`/`PtrToStatic` rejection wholesale when allowing `const_refs_to_static`. That would permit a const to read mutable global memory, e.g. `const READ_MUT: u32 = unsafe { MUTABLE };`, or to hold a reference into mutable memory, e.g. `const C: &i32 = unsafe { &S_MUT };`. Such a const no longer behaves as if inlined and executed at runtime, and a valtree/const pattern could observe a value that may change. The corrected transformation conditions the read check on `alloc.mutability == Mutability::Mut` and rejects `ConstAccessesMutGlobal`; valtree construction refuses non-read-only data; const validation descends into referenced statics and rejects `ConstRefToMutable` and `ConstRefToExtern`.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust const contexts (const initializers, const-fn bodies, type-level consts) with `#![feature(const_refs_to_static)]` that mention or read `static` items. Relevant static kinds: immutable `static`, `static mut`, immutable-declared statics with interior mutability (`SyncUnsafeCell`, `AtomicUsize`), and `extern` statics. Also consts containing references/raw pointers used in pattern matching or valtree conversion. Static initializers are a separate domain: they are allowed to access mutable global memory because they do not need to behave as if executed at runtime.
analysis.trigger: A const initializer or const fn references or reads a `static`, especially a mutable or interior-mutable static; or a const value containing a reference is converted to a valtree or used as a match pattern. The old behavior emitted `constant accesses static`; the corrected behavior allows immutable static reads but emits `constant accesses mutable global memory` for mutable reads and validation errors for const final values referencing mutable/extern statics.
preconditions: The const references a static, so the `const_refs_to_static` feature gate is involved; without the feature the reference is a feature-gate error.
Evaluation is happening in a const context, not a static initializer: the machine flag is `CanAccessMutGlobal::No`.
For pattern/valtree use, the const must successfully convert to a valtree; valtree construction requires the value and everything it refers to to be immutable.
Validation of a const value must recursively inspect referenced statics; static initializers may skip recursive inspection.
pitfalls: Blanket rejection of all static access is too strong: reading an immutable static in a const is allowed under `const_refs_to_static` and is covered by the run-pass test `const_refs_to_static.rs`.
Allowing all static access is unsound: reads from `static mut` or interior-mutable statics must be rejected because their value can differ at runtime.

Creating a pointer/reference is not the same as reading through it. `const C2: *const i32 = unsafe { std::ptr::addr_of!(S_MUT) };` is allowed, but `const C2_READ: () = unsafe { assert!(*C2 == 0); };` must fail with `constant accesses mutable global memory`.

Validation, not just evaluation, must reject const final values that point into mutable memory; otherwise const pattern matching can observe mutable data. The test expects `constructing invalid value: encountered reference to mutable memory in `const``.
Extern statics cannot be validated at compile time; a const value referencing an `extern` static must be rejected (`ConstRefToExtern`) rather than silently accepted.
Do not copy the static-initializer rule to consts: statics may read mutable global memory, consts may not.
Do not conflate the feature-gate diagnostics change (E0013 to E0658) with the semantic permission; the feature still must be enabled and the mutability checks still apply.
analysis.testStrategy: Use focused UI tests pairing programs that differ only in static mutability/read behavior. Positive run-pass case: declare `static S: i32 = 0;`, `const C1: &i32 = &S;`, a const assertion `assert!(*C1 == 0)`, and `assert!(matches!(&0, C1));`. Negative const-eval case: declare `static mut S_MUT: i32 = 0;`, take a pointer with `addr_of!`, then dereference it in another const and require `constant accesses mutable global memory`. Negative validation/pattern case: `const C: &i32 = unsafe { &S_MUT };` must report `encountered reference to mutable memory in `const`` and matching `C` must report `could not evaluate constant pattern`. Add an interior-mutable static (`SyncUnsafeCell`) and an `extern "C" { static S: i8; }` reference to cover `ConstRefToMutable` and `ConstRefToExtern`. Also test without the feature gate that `const C1: &i32 = &S;` is a feature-gate error. Keep const tests separate from static-initializer tests that are allowed to read mutable globals.
evidence: unstably allow constants to refer to statics and read from immutable statics
What we really need is that constants do not *read from* statics that can change their value

This would break the principle that "constants behave as-if their expression was inlined everywhere and executed at runtime". This is enforced by halting const-eval interpretation when a read from a mutable global occurs.

When building a valtree we want to be sure that the constant and everything it refers to is truly immutable. This is enforced by aborting valtree construction when a read from a mutable global occurs.
we ensure that only immutable global memory can be accessed.
For consts on the other hand we have to recursively check;
assert!(*C2 == 0); //~ERROR evaluation of constant value failed
const TEST: u8 = MY_STATIC; //~ ERROR constant
// Computing this pattern will read from an immutable static. That's fine.
